lessons.title: The photoelectric effect
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — quantum physics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the observations of the photoelectric effect and explain why the wave model fails
Use Einstein's equation hf = φ + K_max, the threshold frequency and the stopping potential
Determine the Planck constant from a graph of stopping potential against frequency
reviewNotes: Constants used: e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s; mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m.
φ for sodium varies with sources (about 2.3 eV); state the value in class.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Observations
blocks.md:
When light or ultraviolet radiation falls on a clean metal surface, electrons may be emitted (**photoelectrons**). Observations:

- No emission below a **threshold frequency** f₀ whatever the intensity.
- Above f₀ emission is instantaneous, even at very low intensity.
- The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons depends on the frequency, not on the intensity.
- The number emitted per second is proportional to the intensity.

blocks.title: Einstein's photon model
blocks.md:
Light consists of **photons**, each of energy **E = hf** (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s). One photon gives all its energy to one electron. Part (the **work function** φ) is needed to escape the metal; the rest is kinetic energy:

**hf = φ + K_max**, with φ = hf₀. The **stopping potential** V_s satisfies eV_s = K_max.

blocks.caption: Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against frequency (sodium, φ = 2.3 eV): zero below f₀, then a straight line of gradient h.
blocks.alt: A graph that is flat at zero up to the threshold frequency near 5.5 times 10 to the 14 hertz and then rises in a straight line.

blocks.title: Why the wave model fails
blocks.md:
A wave model predicts that a stronger beam should give electrons more energy, that any frequency should work given enough time, and that there would be a delay while energy builds up. None of this is observed. The photon model explains the threshold, the instant emission and the dependence on frequency.

1 electronvolt (eV) = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J: the energy gained by an electron through 1 V.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Thinking a brighter beam below the threshold frequency can release electrons: it cannot.
- Mixing eV and joules in hf = φ + K: convert consistently.
- Reading the intercept of the V_s–f graph as φ: the y-intercept is −φ/e, the x-intercept is f₀, the gradient is h/e.
- Saying intensity affects the maximum kinetic energy: it affects only the number of electrons.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Sodium
blocks.statement: Sodium has a work function of 2.3 eV (a textbook value). Find the threshold frequency and then K_max and the stopping potential for ultraviolet light of wavelength 300 nm.
blocks.answer: f₀ = 5.55 × 10¹⁴ Hz; K_max = 1.84 eV; V_s = 1.84 V

blocks.title: Example 2 — Planck constant from data
blocks.statement: A student finds V_s = 1.01 V at f = 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and V_s = 2.26 V at f = 11.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Estimate h.
steps: Since eV_s = hf − φ, the gradient of V_s against f is h/e.

lessons.title: Wave–particle duality and line spectra
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — quantum physics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use the de Broglie relation λ = h/p and describe electron diffraction as evidence for matter waves
Explain line spectra using energy levels and use hf = E₂ − E₁ with the hydrogen levels E_n = −13.6/n² eV
Distinguish emission and absorption spectra and describe their uses
reviewNotes: Constants used: e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s; mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m.
Ionisation energy and level formula are given for hydrogen only. Lasers (stimulated emission) and X-ray spectra are not covered; check the syllabus.
The calculated 658 nm differs from the measured 656 nm because of rounding of constants.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Matter waves
blocks.md:
Particles show wave behaviour: the **de Broglie wavelength** of a particle of momentum p = mv is **λ = h/p**. The diffraction of electrons by a thin crystal or graphite shows rings like those of X-rays: this is evidence for the wave nature of matter.

For an electron accelerated from rest through V volts: p = √(2m_eeV), so λ = h/√(2m_eeV). For everyday objects λ is far too small to observe.

blocks.title: Energy levels
blocks.md:
In an atom the electrons occupy discrete **energy levels**. In hydrogen the energy of level n is **E_n = −13.6/n² eV** (n = 1 is the ground state; ionisation energy 13.6 eV).

When an electron falls from a higher level to a lower one, one photon is emitted: **hf = E_upper − E_lower**, so λ = hc/ΔE. Absorption of a photon of exactly this energy raises the electron to the higher level.

blocks.caption: Energy levels of hydrogen and two transitions.
blocks.alt: A ladder of horizontal energy levels from n = 1 at −13.6 electron-volts to n = infinity at zero with two downward arrows labelled 656 nm and 122 nm.

blocks.title: Spectra
blocks.md: A hot low-pressure gas emits an **emission line spectrum**: bright lines of definite wavelengths, characteristic of the element. White light passing through a cool gas gives an **absorption spectrum** (dark lines at the same wavelengths). Line spectra prove that atomic energy levels are discrete and are used to identify elements (for example in stars). A continuous spectrum comes from hot solids.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Taking E_n as positive: bound-state energies are negative.
- Using ΔE in eV in λ = hc/ΔE without converting to joules.
- Saying electrons are 'either waves or particles': both models are needed.
- Thinking the photon energy depends on which level the electron starts from alone: it depends on the difference between two levels.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Electron wavelength
blocks.statement: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through 100 V.
steps: λ = h/p = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ ÷ 5.40 × 10⁻²⁴ = 1.23 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, about the size of an atom, so crystals diffract it.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Hydrogen line
blocks.statement: An electron in hydrogen falls from n = 3 to n = 2. Find the photon energy and wavelength.
steps: λ = hc/ΔE = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 3.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.58 × 10⁻⁷ m = 658 nm (red; the measured line is 656 nm).
